sections.title: Clinical Definition & Overview
sections.content: Corneal graft rejection is an immunological response of the host against the donor corneal tissue. It is a Type IV (delayed-type) hypersensitivity reaction and remains the most common cause of corneal graft failure. Unlike 'Primary Graft Failure' (which occurs within 24-48h due to poor donor quality), rejection requires a prior sensitization period of at least 2 weeks.

sections.title: Pathophysiological Mechanisms
content: Step 1: Afferent Path - Host APCs (dendritic cells) recognize donor MHC Class I and II antigens.
Step 2: Sensitization - APCs migrate to regional lymph nodes to activate T-helper (CD4+) and Cytotoxic T-cells (CD8+).
Step 3: Effector Path - Activated T-cells return to the graft via the limbal vasculature.
Step 4: Target Destruction - T-cells release cytokines (IFN-gamma, IL-2) and directly attack donor endothelium/epithelium/stroma.
Step 5: Angiogenic Switch - Pre-existing corneal vascularization breaks the 'immune privilege' by providing a direct route for T-cell infiltration.

MOST CRITICAL. Causes irreversible loss of donor cells.

sections.title: Emergency 'Red Flags'
content: Sudden drop in BCVA in a previously clear graft
New onset limbal injection/ciliary flush
The presence of a Khodadoust line (linear KPs)
New onset of stromal thickening (>10% increase)
Broken or loose sutures with associated infiltration

sections.title: Diagnostic Workup & Imaging
content: Slit Lamp Exam: Essential for KPs, Khodadoust line, and AC cell/flare grading.
AS-OCT: To quantify corneal thickness (pachymetry) and detect retrocorneal membranes.
Specular Microscopy: To monitor donor endothelial cell density (ECD) loss.
In Vivo Confocal Microscopy (IVCM): Visualizes activated keratocytes and inflammatory cell infiltration at the cellular level.
Intraocular Pressure (IOP): Crucial as steroid-response glaucoma is a common confounder.

rows: Usually bilateral, no specific graft-host junction focus.
High IOP, corneal edema but NO KPs/rejection line.

branches: Stromal: Lattice (High recurrence), Granular, Macular (Least risk)
Posterior: Fuchs (Low rejection in DMEK), PPCD
Ectatic: Keratoconus (Lowest rejection risk - 'Low Risk' eyes)

sections.title: Standard Management Protocol
content: 1. Intensive Topical Steroids: Prednisolone Acetate 1% or Dexamethasone 0.1% every hour (day and night).
2. Pulse Therapy: If severe, consider Methylprednisolone 500mg - 1g IV daily for 3 days.
3. Sub-conjunctival Injection: Betamethasone or Dexamethasone 4mg/1ml for sustained local levels.
4. Systemic Immunosuppression: Cyclosporine A (3-5mg/kg/day), Tacrolimus (0.05-0.1mg/kg/day), or Mycophenolate Mofetil (1g BID) for high-risk grafts.
5. Cycloplegia: Homatropine 5% or Atropine 1% for comfort and stabilization of blood-aqueous barrier.

sections.title: Surgical Nuances: PKP vs. EK
content: PKP: Highest risk due to full-thickness antigen load and sutures.
DSAEK: Moderate risk; rejection often presents as localized swelling without classic line.
DMEK: Lowest rejection risk (approx. 1%) due to minimal stromal/antigenic tissue transfer.
DALK: Avoids endothelial rejection entirely; only epithelial/stromal rejection possible.

sections.title: Clinical Pearls & Landmark Studies
content: CCTS Study: HLA matching did NOT significantly reduce rejection in high-risk grafts, but ABO compatibility might.
Steroid Taper: Never taper steroids faster than 1 drop/month once the rejection has resolved.
High Risk Factors: >2 quadrants of neovascularization, previous graft failure, active inflammation.
Epithelial rejection is a 'warning shot'—intensify topical steroids immediately.
